title: Holika Dahan: the boy in the fire
hook: the night before the colors: a boy who wouldn't stop saying the name, and the fire that couldn't burn him
carry: bhakti: prahlada held the name, and it held him

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diwali ended: Lakshmi at the open door, a hill lifted over everyone, a sister's blessing. Your line was Krishna shelters everyone who comes under.

The famous photos of Holi show people drenched in pink and green and yellow powder, laughing in the street. But that's the morning. The night before, in towns and villages and temple courtyards, people gather around a great pile of wood and dried branches, sometimes with a figure set on top. At the right moment, it's lit, and the flames go up into the full-moon sky. People walk around it, throw in grain and coconuts, and hold up stalks of fresh wheat to roast. And somebody's grandmother tells the story, again, about a little boy who sat in a fire and walked out.
screen: `BEFORE THE COLORS, A BONFIRE.` → `THE FULL MOON, THE FLAMES.` → `A BOY WHO WALKED OUT OF THE FIRE.`

segments.voice: It starts with a demon king, Hiranyakashipu. After years of fierce austerity, he wins an extraordinary protection: he can't be killed by man or beast, by day or by night, indoors or outdoors, on the ground or in the air, by any weapon. Believing himself unkillable, he orders everyone to worship him. Everyone does, except his own small son, Prahlada. Asked what the best thing he's learned is, the boy answers: hearing about Vishnu, singing his names, remembering him. The Bhagavata Purana says his father tries poison, elephants, snakes, a cliff; each time the boy is kept safe. Then comes the part told at Holi bonfires. The king's sister, Holika, is protected against fire. She takes Prahlada onto her lap and sits in a blazing pyre. And the fire goes the other way. Holika burns. Prahlada walks out untouched, still saying the name. Said plainly: the Bhagavata doesn't tell the Holika episode; it lives in other retellings and in the festival itself. Soon after, Vishnu comes as Narasimha, half man, half lion, and ends the king's cruelty. Here's the teaching. Prahlada is bhakti's model devotee, and his answer begins the classic list of ways Hindus love God. Saying the name is the simplest, and the story says it's a refuge no tyrant can take. So the bonfire is Holika Dahan, the burning of Holika. People circle it, as on day one hundred thirty-four, toss in new grain, and call it good's victory over evil.
screen: `A KING WHO THOUGHT HE COULDN'T DIE.` · `A SON WHO WOULDN'T STOP SAYING THE NAME.` · `HOLIKA BURNS; PRAHLADA WALKS OUT.` · `BHAKTI: HEAR, SING, REMEMBER.` · then, large: `HOLIKA DAHAN: THE BONFIRE.`

segments.voice: Picture the bonfire, the heat on your face, the full moon above. Name one thing you'd like to put on it, a grudge, a fear, a habit of cruelty, and watch it burn to ash. Then do what Prahlada did. If you pray, say a name you love, Ram, Krishna, or Om Namo Narayanaya, once with each breath, even with all the noise around you. If you don't, hold one true thing you won't trade away.
Holi. The spring festival that begins the night before, with a bonfire for Prahlada, the boy the fire couldn't burn. Today's word.
Your line: bhakti. Prahlada held the name, and it held him. Tomorrow, the colors come out. That's day one hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: On the full-moon night before Holi, many Hindu communities light a bonfire for Holika Dahan, retelling the story of Prahlada, walking around the fire, offering grain and coconut, and roasting new wheat or barley; the colors are played the next morning.

original.note: Sanskrit/Hindi holikā: the aunt in the story, and the bonfire named for her, Holika Dahan.

trapdoor: what you thought: a festival of colored powder.
what it means: a spring festival that starts with a bonfire for Prahlada, bhakti's model devotee, whose love for God's name outlasted a tyrant and a fire.

what a scholar hears: Prahlada and Narasimha are told in Bhagavata Purana 7.2–10, and Prahlada's list of nine ways of devotion (hearing, singing, remembering…) is at 7.5.23–24; the Holika episode belongs to later Puranic and folk tradition, and Holika Dahan on the Phalguna full moon also marks the spring harvest with roasted grain.
